title: The ketubah read
hook: the marriage contract is read aloud under the chuppah

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chuppah, and your line was a house open on all sides. Who did you let in? Today, under that open roof, someone unfolds a document and starts to read. Day one thousand three hundred six.

Under the canopy, the music has stopped. The couple stands close. Someone steps forward with a large sheet of paper, sometimes plain, sometimes painted with flowers, birds, a border of Hebrew letters. And they begin to read aloud, in Aramaic. Some guests follow every word. Some only hear the rhythm. At some weddings a translation comes after. What's being read isn't a poem. It's a contract, with obligations and a sum of money in it. Why stop a wedding, at the moment everyone is waiting for, to read out a legal document?
screen: `THE MUSIC STOPS.` → `A DOCUMENT, READ IN ARAMAIC.` → `A CONTRACT, AT A WEDDING?`

segments.voice: The ketubah, read aloud. Turn it four ways. First, the name. Ketubah means, simply, the written thing. It is the marriage contract, and it sets out what the husband owes his wife. Second, where those duties come from. In Exodus, in a law about a man who takes a second wife, the Torah lists what he may not hold back from the first. In the King James wording: "her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish." Food, clothing, and closeness. The rabbis read that verse as a floor, not a ceiling: the least a marriage owes, written down so no one can pretend it was never said. Third, the protection. The ketubah also promises the wife a sum of money if the marriage ends, by divorce or by her husband's death. The Talmud gives the reason: so that a husband couldn't send his wife away lightly. In a world where a woman could be left with nothing, the rabbis put a cost on leaving and her name on the page. Fourth, why aloud. The ketubah is signed by witnesses before the ceremony, and then it's read in front of everyone. A promise read out in a crowd is a promise the crowd can remember. Some hang their ketubah on a wall at home. And some couples today choose a ketubah with promises from both sides, in words they've thought through together. Either way, the idea under the canopy is the same. Love is the reason. The writing is how it gets kept.
screen: `THE WRITTEN THING.` · `FOOD, CLOTHING, AND CLOSENESS.` · `A COST ON LEAVING.` · `READ IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` · then, large: `PROMISED IN WRITING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one promise aloud. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one promise you've made. It might be written down somewhere, or only spoken, or only meant: to a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, yourself. Put it into one plain sentence. Then, if you're somewhere you can, say it quietly out loud, as if it were being read under a canopy. Hear it outside your own head. Notice how it sounds, and whether you're keeping it. Then let it rest, and stay with your breath. The bell holds the time.
The ketubah read: the marriage contract, signed by witnesses and read aloud under the chuppah, so the promise is heard as well as written. Today's word.
Your line: promised in writing. Today, write down one promise you mean to keep, and put it where you'll see it. Day one thousand three hundred six.

howItsDone: Before a Jewish wedding, witnesses sign the ketubah, the marriage contract; under the chuppah it is read aloud, traditionally in Aramaic, often followed by a translation, and some couples later display it at home.

original.note: Hebrew: the written thing, the marriage contract; Ashkenazi Jews often say keh-SU-bah.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ketubah is a pretty certificate to frame.
what it means: a binding contract of a husband's duties, signed by witnesses and read aloud.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 21:10's food, raiment and duty of marriage, and the Talmud's reason for the ketubah sum: so divorce isn't taken lightly.

sources.quoted: her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish.

notes: Exodus 21:10 quoted from the KJV; confirm wording. JPS 1917 reads 'conjugal rights' (unverified), so the KJV was used.
Ketubah from the root k-t-v (write), 'the written thing': standard, but an etymology; confirm or cut.
The Talmud's reason for the ketubah sum ('so that it not be easy in his eyes to send her away'): cited as Ketubot 11a / 39b and Yevamot 89a; confirm the best reference.

The rabbinic reading of Exodus 21:10 as the husband's obligations (food, clothing, conjugal duty) to a wife: the verse in context concerns a maidservant-wife; the rabbis generalized it (cf. Mishnah Ketubot 5:6–9, Ketubot 47b–48a). Confirm framing ('the rabbis read that verse as a floor').

'Signed by witnesses before the ceremony', 'at many weddings an English summary comes after', 'many couples hang their ketubah', and 'some couples choose a ketubah with promises from both sides': confirm. No movement is named for egalitarian ketubot on purpose.
Ashkenazi pronunciation keh-SU-bah in the original note; confirm.

Editor: cut the root claim ('comes from the Hebrew word for writing'), keeping only the plain gloss; Exodus 21:10 now framed in its context (a man taking a second wife) before the rabbis' generalization; varied a repeated 'some couples'.
